learningObjective: Describe the MoE routing pipeline: gating, top-k expert selection, and token dispatch to experts.

canonicalClaims.claim: Top-k MoE: gate scores are computed per token; top-k experts (usually k=2) are selected and normalized to get combining weights; each token contributes to the k selected experts' input batches and only those experts run on that token; outputs are combined weighted by gate scores.
conditions: Load balancing is addressed via auxiliary losses or capacity limits in training/serving.
nonImplications: Does not imply every expert runs on every token.
Does not imply k > 1 requires k separate passes.

misconceptions.claim: MoE runs every expert on every token; sparsity is a soft-masking illusion.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Sparse MoE explicitly avoids running non-selected experts; this is where compute savings come from.

misconceptions.claim: k > 1 MoE requires k full forward passes.
misconceptions.whyWrong: k slots per token are handled in a single grouped dispatch (grouped GEMM or all-to-all).

misconceptions.claim: Only top-1 routing is used in modern MoE.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Both top-1 (Switch) and top-2 (Mixtral, GShard) are widely used.

implementationFacts: Load imbalance: 'expert overloading' triggers token dropping when a capacity factor is exceeded.
In distributed setup, expert parallelism (EP) places experts on different devices and uses all-to-all to shuffle tokens.
performanceScenarios: MoE achieves large parameter count per active flop but at the cost of routing overhead and imbalance risk.
Grouped GEMM (varying tile shapes per expert) is the standard efficient dense-kernel path.
